operationalization: Map eye complexity, optical performance, ecology, and phylogeny across arthropods, then test whether inferred transitions are mostly small and whether intermediate states improve performance. A well-supported phylogenetic sequence lacking viable intermediates would count against the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: comparative morphological matrices for eyes and related structures

obstacles: Living forms are not literal ancestors.
Fitness effects of historical intermediate eyes are usually unmeasured.
rationale: Comparative morphology and phylogenies can test graded transitions and functional plausibility. They cannot directly observe the complete historical path or uniquely attribute it to natural selection.

operationalization: For sampled complex organs, reconstruct ancestral states and test whether each transition can be decomposed into small heritable functional changes. One rigorously established organ requiring an inaccessible discontinuity would refute the universal claim, while finite surveys cannot confirm it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: morphological character matrices for selected organ systems

obstacles: The universal quantifier cannot be confirmed by sampling.
Possibility of a pathway is difficult to establish or exclude.
rationale: Existing data permit case studies but not an exhaustive test over all complex organs. The word 'possibly' also makes decisive discrimination unusually difficult.

operationalization: Combine vertebrate phylogenies with developmental, anatomical, and gene-expression characters for lungs and gas bladders, and reconstruct the ancestral organ and its function. Homology and an ancestral flotation bladder support the claim; independent origins or an ancestral lung refute its stated direction.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus
candidate_datasets.role: public developmental expression data for respiratory and gas-bladder tissues

obstacles: Deep ancestral-state direction can remain model-sensitive.
Functional use in the ancient ancestor is inferred indirectly.
rationale: Modern phylogenomic, developmental, and anatomical data directly address homology and transition direction. The ancient organ's precise flotation function remains less securely recoverable.

operationalization: Place similar organs and their developmental or genetic architectures on independently supported phylogenies and test whether similarity arose on separate branches. Multiple independent origins with convergent function support the claim; homology inherited from one ancestor would refute a proposed case.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: sequence data for independent phylogenies and organ-related genes

obstacles: Deep homology of regulatory components can coexist with organ-level convergence.
rationale: Convergence is routinely tested with phylogenies, morphology, and molecular data. Existing coverage is strong for canonical examples, though not every similar organ.

operationalization: Define a representative inventory of organ systems and score whether extant or fossil taxa exhibit ordered structural grades approaching each system. Estimate the fraction lacking any known grade, with preregistered rules for what counts as transitional.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: fossil occurrences relevant to extinct grades

obstacles: No complete standardized inventory of organs and grades exists.
The terms 'rarely' and 'towards' allow subjective coding.
rationale: A sample-based estimate is possible, but global coverage across plant and animal organs is poor. Coding transitional grades requires substantial interpretation.

operationalization: Partition morphological variation into phylogenetic inheritance and association with current ecology using comparative models across clades. Strong phylogenetic signal after controlling for present habits supports the claim; predominantly ecology-specific structure would oppose it.
obstacles: 'Chief part' lacks a natural unit of measurement.
Inheritance and adaptation are not mutually exclusive explanations.
rationale: Phylogenetic comparative data can quantify inheritance for selected traits and clades. The organism-wide universal and the amount meant by 'chief part' prevent complete resolution.

operationalization: Catalogue interspecific traits and estimate their direct and inclusive-fitness effects on the bearer and beneficiary. A trait with persistent benefit only to another species and no direct or indirect benefit to its bearer would refute the claim.
obstacles: Exclusive absence of bearer benefit is extremely hard to establish.
Interaction databases rarely contain fitness effects.
rationale: Public data can identify candidate mutualisms or exploitative structures but seldom measure all fitness consequences. The universal negative cannot be confirmed exhaustively.

operationalization: Compare establishment, displacement, abundance, and performance of introduced versus endemic species across islands and continents while controlling for propagule pressure and environment. Systematic competitive replacement supports the prediction; endemic superiority under matched conditions opposes it.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Register of Introduced and Invasive Species

obstacles: Propagule pressure and human disturbance confound competitive superiority.
'Perfect' has no single measurable scale.
rationale: Large invasion datasets support broad tests of the island-versus-mainland implication. They test a proxy for local competitive adaptation, not perfection itself or its exclusive production by selection.

operationalization: Reconstruct the origin, ancestral function, and later use of candidate traits on phylogenies, testing whether traits predate the ecology in which they became advantageous. Temporal precedence and later functional recruitment support co-option.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: temporal occurrences of taxa bearing candidate traits

obstacles: Initial absence of advantage is difficult to infer.
'Laws of growth' requires modern reinterpretation.
rationale: Exaptation can be tested for well-documented traits using morphology, fossils, and phylogeny. Existing data cannot establish the proposed initial cause or frequency across 'many modifications.'

operationalization: Define leap size in phenotypic or genetic character space and estimate transition magnitudes through densely sampled fossil and extant lineages. Repeated well-resolved discontinuities without intermediates would oppose strict gradualism.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: fossil occurrence series for candidate transitions

obstacles: The complete history of all organisms is unrecoverable.
Sampling gaps can mimic leaps and flexible timescales can erase them.
rationale: Selected lineages can test rates and apparent discontinuities. A strict statement covering every past organism cannot be confirmed, and missing intermediates are weak evidence of true leaps.

operationalization: Test whether shared structural plans covary with independently inferred common ancestry more strongly than with present ecology, using morphological and molecular phylogenies. Nested homology matching ancestry supports the claim; repeated ecology-based grouping independent of ancestry opposes it.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: molecular data for independent phylogenetic tests

obstacles: Some morphological characters also inform classifications and can create circularity.
rationale: Independent molecular trees and broad morphology directly test whether unity of type tracks descent. Strong existing coverage and standard comparative methods make the central empirical consequence resolvable.

operationalization: For instinctive behaviours with known pedigrees or genomic data, estimate heritable variation, selection, and transgenerational effects of acquired habits. Predominant response through heritable variants rather than inherited acquired behaviour supports the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Sequence Read Archive
candidate_datasets.role: genomic data for behavioural variation in studied species

obstacles: Public behaviour datasets rarely combine pedigrees, selection, and transgenerational experiments.
Relative historical contributions are difficult to reconstruct.
rationale: Modern data can test genetic variation and inheritance for selected behaviours. They do not broadly quantify the historical balance between selection and inherited habit across complex instincts.

operationalization: Code homologous instinct components across related species and reconstruct transition sizes on independent phylogenies. Predominantly ordered, small changes and extant collateral grades support the claim; repeated abrupt origins without component precursors oppose it.
obstacles: Behavioural phenotypes are sparsely standardized.
Collateral living species are not ancestors.
rationale: Comparative tests are feasible for migration and a few other behaviours. Existing datasets lack the breadth and resolution needed for complex instincts generally.

operationalization: Identify interspecific helping behaviours and estimate lifetime direct and inclusive-fitness effects for actor and recipient. A heritable instinct with benefit exclusively to the other species and no compensating actor benefit would refute the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biotic Interactions
candidate_datasets.role: records of mutualistic and other interspecific interactions

obstacles: Databases record interactions, not complete fitness accounting.
Proving zero actor benefit is exceptionally difficult.
rationale: Existing records can screen for candidate behaviours but cannot settle exclusivity for all animals. Focused systems are testable only partially.

operationalization: Measure within-species variation in migration direction, distance, timing, and nest traits among wild individuals and populations. Reproducible within-species variance supports the claim; invariant behaviour across adequately sampled populations refutes each example.
obstacles: Observation effort and tracking-device coverage are uneven.
rationale: The variables are direct and enormous public movement and occurrence datasets exist. Standard analyses can resolve the claim for migration and many bird populations.

operationalization: Relate flight-initiation distance or approach tolerance across populations to quantified duration and intensity of human persecution, controlling for body size, urbanization, and phylogeny. Increasing fear with exposure supports the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Movebank
candidate_datasets.role: movement responses for some tracked populations

obstacles: Flight-initiation measurements are scattered rather than centrally standardized.
Urban habituation and species sorting confound persecution history.
rationale: Many published observations make cross-population tests possible, but the key fear and persecution variables require substantial compilation. Causal acquisition speed remains difficult to isolate.

operationalization: Compare domestic breeds and wild relatives for behavioural phenotypes, genomic selection signals, and experimentally demonstrated transgenerational habit effects. Selection signatures tied to breed histories support human selection; inherited acquired habits would require independent evidence.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal QTLdb
candidate_datasets.role: mapped loci for behavioural and domestication traits

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Sequence Read Archive
candidate_datasets.role: genomes of domestic breeds and wild relatives

obstacles: Historical unconscious selection is poorly recorded.
Darwin's inherited habit mechanism does not map cleanly to modern inheritance.
rationale: Selection on domestic behaviour is testable in several species. Partitioning historical change between selection and inherited habit is not adequately supported by current datasets.

operationalization: Map nest building, facultative egg dumping, and obligate brood parasitism across a cuckoo phylogeny, reconstruct ancestral states, and compare offspring success. The predicted ordered transition and fitness advantage support the claim.
obstacles: Behaviour and reproductive-success data are dispersed across studies.
Ancestral states are model-dependent.
rationale: Comparative evidence can strongly test the proposed sequence, but no single open dataset contains all breeding behaviours and fitness measurements. The exact historical pathway remains inferential.

operationalization: Code predation on pupae, facultative brood capture, worker integration, and obligate dulosis across ant phylogenies, then reconstruct transition order. A progression from food collection to useful rearing supports the claim; different ancestral behaviour opposes it.
obstacles: Behavioural states and fitness consequences require literature compilation.
Multiple origins may have followed different routes.
rationale: The transition is operationalizable through comparative reconstruction. Public centralized data cover taxonomy and phylogeny better than the decisive behavioural sequence.

operationalization: Quantify comb-building behaviours and architectures across bumblebees, stingless bees, and honeybees, then reconstruct ancestral transitions on a bee phylogeny. Ordered small changes toward regular comb support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: morphological character matrices for comparative coding

obstacles: Nest architecture and construction behaviour are not broadly standardized in open databases.
Modern grades do not uniquely establish the historical route.
rationale: A focused synthesis can test whether comparative states fit gradual evolution. Existing open data are incomplete and discriminate imperfectly among alternative historical sequences.

operationalization: Analyze time-resolved imaging and bee trajectories during comb construction for equal spacing, spherical excavation, and wall formation at predicted intersections. Systematic construction by another geometry would refute the mechanism.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: repository containing public behavioural imaging and tracking supplements where deposited

obstacles: The required time-resolved construction datasets are sparse and scattered.
Wax deformation after deposition can obscure initial geometry.
rationale: The mechanism gives precise measurable predictions and could be cleanly tested. Public data exist for limited colonies and imaging studies, but may not provide adequate replication.

operationalization: Measure cell volume, wall area, thickness, mechanical constraints, and wax mass, then compare observed combs with constrained mathematical optima. Any feasible architecture using less wax at equal capacity and strength refutes absolute optimality.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: public repository for deposited comb morphometry and imaging data

obstacles: Absolute optimality depends on constraints such as strength, temperature, and construction error.
Centralized large morphometric datasets are lacking.
rationale: The claim is quantitatively falsifiable and standard optimization methods suffice. Existing measurements permit limited tests, but full biological constraints and broad colony coverage are incomplete.

operationalization: Estimate heritability of worker traits through reproductive parents and test whether colony reproductive output increases with those traits. A genetic association transmitted by breeders plus colony-level fitness effects supports family selection.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Sequence Read Archive
candidate_datasets.role: genomic data from social-insect colonies and castes

obstacles: Colony fitness and pedigree data are concentrated in model species.
Kin and multilevel-selection parameterizations can describe the same process.
rationale: Modern quantitative genetics and social-evolution data directly establish how sterile-worker traits respond to selection through relatives. Broad taxonomic coverage is imperfect but sufficient to resolve the mechanism.

operationalization: Measure worker morphology within nests and test whether trait distributions contain continuous or graded intermediates between worker forms. Frequent within-nest intermediates support the prediction; consistently discrete distributions across adequately sampled species oppose it.

candidate_datasets.name: AntWeb
candidate_datasets.role: digitized ant specimens and worker morphology

obstacles: Specimen records may not always preserve nest identity.
Developmental plasticity can produce grades without documenting their evolutionary origin.
rationale: The stated morphological prediction is direct and testable with specimen images and measurements. The observation alone does not prove the proposed selection mechanism, but it resolves the prediction.

operationalization: Map continuous and discrete worker polymorphisms on ant phylogenies and model whether discrete castes derive from graded ancestors, while testing colony performance of extremes versus intermediates. The predicted transition and fitness pattern support the claim.
obstacles: Historical loss of intermediates is reconstructed rather than observed.
Colony performance data are not centralized.
rationale: Morphological transitions can be tested comparatively in sampled ants. Existing data are weaker for the asserted selective advantage and exact elimination process.

operationalization: Quantify behavioural similarity among close relatives occupying different environments and compare phylogenetic versus environmental effects. Strong behavioural phylogenetic signal after environmental control supports inherited instinct.
obstacles: Many instincts lack standardized cross-species measurements.
Similar unmeasured ecological pressures can mimic inheritance.
rationale: Phylogenetic comparative analyses are straightforward for behaviours represented in movement datasets. Coverage is too narrow to resolve the generalization over allied animals.

operationalization: Separate fertilization or F1-production success from fertility of surviving F1 hybrids and compare their physiological causes. Distinct failure stages and mechanisms support the claimed distinction.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: public cross and hybrid-fertility datasets deposited by studies

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive-tissue expression in hybrids and parents

obstacles: Crossing records are dispersed and taxonomically biased.
rationale: The two outcomes are standard, separately measured reproductive-isolation components. Existing experimental datasets resolve the distinction even though no comprehensive cross-taxon database exists.

operationalization: Model fertility and offspring viability against pedigree inbreeding coefficients and genetic distance of mates, including hybrid lineages across generations. Decline under close inbreeding and recovery after outcrossing support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal QTLdb
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive traits and mapped genetic factors in managed animals

obstacles: Effects vary among taxa and genetic backgrounds.
Hybrid decline can also reflect segregation and incompatibilities.
rationale: Inbreeding depression and heterosis are directly measurable with many public pedigrees and experiments. Standard mixed models can resolve the broad directional claim while testing alternative hybrid mechanisms.

operationalization: For domestic lineages with multiple wild progenitors, compare present cross fertility with wild-source crosses and identify changes associated with domestication. Repeated evolved restoration of fertility supports removability.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Sequence Read Archive
candidate_datasets.role: genomes of domestic lineages and proposed wild progenitors

obstacles: Many domestic-origin claims involve populations rather than distinct species.
Historical ancestral sterility is seldom directly measured.
rationale: Current fertility and ancestry are testable, but Darwin's premise about distinct progenitor species is often uncertain. Existing data only indirectly show that domestication removed an earlier barrier.

operationalization: Compile attempted interspecific crosses and estimate the frequency and degree of reduced F1 production and F1 fertility relative to within-species controls. High but non-unit prevalence supports the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: genetic distances and taxonomy for crossed species

obstacles: Failed and null crosses are underreported.
Available crosses are a highly selected taxonomic sample.
rationale: Outcomes are measurable, but no complete public census of attempted crosses exists. Publication and experiment-selection biases prevent a secure estimate over plants and animals generally.

operationalization: For species pairs with both measurements, correlate first-cross success with fertility of their F1 offspring and quantify residual variation. A positive but far-from-perfect association supports the claim.
obstacles: Paired measurements are scattered.
Successful-cross ascertainment biases estimates of hybrid sterility.
rationale: The proposed correlation is direct and statistically simple. Public data can resolve it within studied groups, but broad paired coverage is incomplete and biased.

operationalization: Regress first-cross and hybrid fertility on independently estimated phylogenetic distance across species pairs, allowing clade-specific effects. A strong negative but imperfect relationship supports the claim.
obstacles: Cross-outcome data are incomplete and biased toward close relatives.
The categorical family-level assertion is difficult to sample comprehensively.
rationale: Standard comparative models can test affinity effects and exceptions. Data coverage supports multiple clade-level analyses but not the full scope across plants and animals.

operationalization: Compare fertilization, offspring number, and viability in both reciprocal directions for the same species pairs. Large repeatable direction effects support the claim; symmetry across well-powered pairs opposes it.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: reciprocal-cross datasets from plant and animal studies

obstacles: Cross records are decentralized and taxonomically uneven.
rationale: Reciprocal crossing is a direct controlled comparison with strong discriminating power. Numerous public datasets allow immediate resolution of the phenomenon, though not exhaustive prevalence estimation.

operationalization: Test whether hybrid sterility is mechanistically explained by mapped reproductive incompatibilities and whether those variants show evidence of selection specifically to prevent gene flow. Incidental pleiotropic incompatibilities support the claim; consistent barrier-specific adaptation opposes it.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Sequence Read Archive
candidate_datasets.role: population genomic data for selection tests

obstacles: Absence of historical purpose is not directly measurable.
Reinforcement can specially strengthen barriers after incidental incompatibilities arise.
rationale: Mechanisms of incompatibility and signatures of reinforcement are empirically testable. The teleological contrast 'specially endowed' has no unique modern measurement, limiting discrimination.

operationalization: Stage reciprocal interspecific crosses and classify failure as pre-fertilization, embryonic death, later mortality, or adult sterility. Estimate the fraction of first-cross infertility attributable to early embryo death.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus
candidate_datasets.role: hybrid embryo expression and developmental failure data

obstacles: Negative and failed crosses are underreported.
'Very frequent' requires representative sampling across taxa.
rationale: Failure stage is directly observable and many datasets document hybrid embryogenesis. Biased and incomplete taxonomic coverage prevents reliable resolution of the claimed general frequency.

operationalization: Compare reproductive output, general-health measures, gonadal pathology, and expression profiles between hybrids and pure species exposed to captivity or environmental stress. Shared reproductive-specific disruption supports the proposed resemblance.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive-tissue expression under hybridization and environmental stress

obstacles: Phenotypic resemblance does not establish a shared causal mechanism.
'Unnatural conditions' covers heterogeneous treatments.
rationale: Parallel reproductive phenotypes and molecular pathways can be compared with existing datasets. Confounding and Darwin's broad environmental category make the causal analogy only partly resolvable.

operationalization: Estimate nonlinear responses of fitness and fertility to environmental displacement and parental genetic distance. Peaks at modest environmental change and modest outcrossing, with declines at extremes, support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: environmental and geographic context for source populations

obstacles: Optimal change depends strongly on taxon and baseline environment.
Environmental and genetic effects are usually studied separately.
rationale: The predicted hump-shaped relationships are testable in many experiments. Existing data do not adequately cover Darwin's universal scope or jointly measure both parallels.

operationalization: Compare fertility of crosses among named varieties with within-variety controls and identify any reproducible partial sterility. A single robust counterexample refutes universality; prevalence estimates test 'very general.'

candidate_datasets.name: GRIN-Global
candidate_datasets.role: germplasm and accession information for cultivated varieties

obstacles: Variety definitions differ among studies.
Crossing failures are less likely to be published or deposited.
rationale: Universality is readily falsifiable and public experiments contain counterexample candidates. Estimating general prevalence across natural and domestic varieties remains data-limited.

operationalization: Measure phenotypic variance in F1, F2, and later hybrid generations under common conditions, then compare generation-specific variance. Low F1 and substantially higher segregating-generation variance support the claim.
obstacles: Environmental variance and parental divergence affect contrasts.
The proposed cause is less directly tested than the variance pattern.
rationale: Generation-specific segregation variance is a standard quantitative-genetic measurement with many public mapping populations. The pattern is resolvable now, while Darwin's causal wording is only partly addressed.

operationalization: Using matched crosses, compare hybrids and within-species variety crosses for phenotypic variance, parental resemblance, transmission distortion or prepotency, and reversion. Similar effect-size distributions after excluding fertility support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: public interspecific and intraspecific cross datasets

obstacles: Prepotency and reversion lack uniform modern metrics.
Matched species and variety crosses are uncommon.
rationale: Several components can be compared with existing genetic crosses, but the composite assertion requires substantial harmonization. Broad plant-and-animal coverage is inadequate.

operationalization: No unique dataset-level test exists until 'fundamental distinction' is defined; one could instead test whether reproductive isolation, genomic divergence, and gene flow form a continuum across named varieties and species.
obstacles: Species and variety are classification concepts with multiple definitions.
Continuity in measured traits does not settle whether a distinction is fundamental.
rationale: Genomic datasets can demonstrate continua and clusters, but neither outcome uniquely resolves the philosophical taxonomic conclusion. The claim lacks a fixed empirical decision criterion as stated.

operationalization: For related living species, infer their common ancestor on independent phylogenies and test whether fossil or reconstructed intermediates lie along separate stem lineages rather than morphologically midway between the living tips. The predicted branching pattern supports the claim.
obstacles: True ancestors are rarely identifiable as such.
Fossil sampling is uneven.
rationale: The branching rather than ladder-like prediction is directly testable across many well-sampled clades. Public phylogenetic and fossil data are extensive, though ancestral identity remains probabilistic.

operationalization: Estimate numbers and morphological spacing of unsampled ancestral lineages from dated phylogenies, fossil occurrence rates, and diversification models. Large inferred missing lineage counts support the qualitative claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: observed fossil diversity and sampling rates

obstacles: 'Inconceivably great' has no numerical threshold.
Most extinct lineages and morphologies are unobserved.
rationale: Models can estimate missing diversity and transition counts for clades. The global magnitude and stipulated small phenotypic steps are not directly recoverable, and the key adjective is vague.

operationalization: Date the late Chalk and the denudation history of the Weald with radiometric ages, stratigraphy, geomorphology, and erosion models, then compare elapsed time with 300 million years. An interval below that value refutes the estimate.

candidate_datasets.name: British Geological Survey Geology of Britain Viewer
candidate_datasets.role: official geology and stratigraphy of the Weald

obstacles: Reconstructing denudation rate is model-dependent, but the elapsed-time claim is not.
rationale: Modern geochronology directly and precisely dates the interval since the Late Cretaceous. Public geological data and standard methods decisively resolve Darwin's numerical claim.

operationalization: Compare preservation frequencies by tissue mineralization and depositional regime, and test for wholly soft-bodied fossils and skeletal remains in condensed or nondepositional settings. Verified soft-bodied fossils directly refute the absolute first clause, while taphonomic patterns test the bias.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: fossil occurrences, environments, and taxonomic composition

obstacles: Exceptional preservation creates strong site-selection effects.
Absence of preservation is difficult to distinguish from absence of organisms.
rationale: Soft-bodied fossil occurrences and taphonomic associations are directly documented in public data. The absolute non-preservation statement is readily falsifiable and the broader bias can be quantified.

operationalization: Quantify hiatus durations between mapped sedimentary packages and decompose estimated fossil-record incompleteness among nondeposition or erosion, preservation failure, and sampling. Dominance of long inter-formational hiatuses supports the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Macrostrat
candidate_datasets.role: global stratigraphic packages, ages, and hiatuses

obstacles: The relative importance of causes varies by region and taxon.
Hiatus duration and fossil incompleteness have correlated estimation errors.
rationale: Large public stratigraphic and fossil databases permit explicit quantification of hiatuses and sampling. The word 'mainly' requires modeling choices but is empirically assessable.

operationalization: Relate formation thickness, fossil richness, depositional depth, tectonic subsidence histories, and sediment accumulation rates. Concentration of thick fossil-rich units in slowly subsiding shallow basins with accommodation matched by sediment supports the mechanism.

candidate_datasets.name: Macrostrat
candidate_datasets.role: formation thickness, ages, lithology, and basin context

obstacles: Present thickness reflects compaction and later erosion.
Subsidence histories require regional models.
rationale: The predicted geological associations are measurable at broad scale with public data. Standard basin and comparative analyses can distinguish subsidence from alternative settings.

operationalization: Align regional uplift and subsidence histories with origination, extinction, and fossil-deposition rates, correcting for sampling. Elevation-associated origination and subsidence-associated extinction and fossil richness support the linked prediction.
obstacles: Rock availability directly biases inferred diversity rates.
Elevation and subsidence are spatially heterogeneous and difficult to align with populations.
rationale: Existing databases support broad temporal association tests. Preservation bias is entangled with the proposed biological rates, limiting causal discrimination.

operationalization: Compare durations of formations with independently estimated species-transition durations and measure the frequency of within-formation ancestor-descendant morphological series. Predominantly shorter formations and rare complete series support the claim.
obstacles: Formation boundaries and durations vary regionally.
Speciation duration is hard to estimate independently of fossil sampling.
rationale: Formation duration and fossil occurrence are well represented, but transformation time and complete graded series are harder to measure. Tests are informative yet substantially confounded by temporal resolution.

operationalization: For regional first appearances within formations, compare local first-occurrence dates with older occurrences elsewhere and use phylogeographic or occupancy models to classify immigration versus local origination. A majority with prior external records supports the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Macrostrat
candidate_datasets.role: regional formation ages and stratigraphic context

obstacles: The true source area may be unsampled.
Age uncertainty can reverse apparent first appearances.
rationale: Georeferenced fossil occurrences allow explicit comparison of regional and global first appearances. Preservation and dating biases remain, but standard occupancy and sensitivity analyses can test the probabilistic generalization.
